questions.q: Why does Theo run one combined game-day drill instead of testing each Lesson 23 change separately?
options: Because separate tests take too long to schedule
Because the changes are meant to work together under real load during a scheduled capacity change, and that's exactly the condition nobody fully tested before the original incident
Because combined drills are cheaper to run
Because Casey required exactly one test
questions.explain: Each change passing in isolation wouldn't prove they hold up together under the real combined condition — which was the actual gap before the original incident.

questions.q: Why are the drill's pass conditions decided BEFORE the drill runs, rather than judged afterward?
options: It doesn't matter when they're decided
So there's no room to quietly redefine 'success' after seeing the results — it keeps the exercise a real validation rather than a story told after the fact
Because Dana requires a signed form in advance
Because the pipeline script requires it
questions.explain: Pre-defined, measurable pass conditions are what separates an actual validation from after-the-fact rationalization.

questions.q: What does the controlled node drain step in the drill actually test?
options: Whether the autoscaler can be disabled
Whether the PodDisruptionBudget blocks enough simultaneous evictions during a drain to avoid a capacity gap and an error-rate increase
Whether the FinOps dashboard renders correctly
Whether Terraform can delete a node pool
questions.explain: The drain step specifically validates the new PodDisruptionBudget added in Lesson 23 under a real, deliberately triggered disruption.

questions.q: What real finding did the drill actually produce?
options: The autoscaler failed to reach the new ceiling
The failover cutover to the secondary cloud landed a few seconds past the originally planned RTO, within an acceptable margin but not instant
The per-AZ dashboard panel stopped working
The budget anomaly alert never fired
questions.explain: The drill's one real finding was a minor RTO margin on failover, logged as a documented follow-up since it still met the 'within planned RTO' pass condition.

questions.q: Why is a drill that surfaces a small, specific finding considered a BETTER outcome than a drill with zero findings?
options: Because zero findings always means the drill was run incorrectly
Because a small, documented fact discovered on a controlled schedule beats discovering the same fact for the first time during a real failover under real pressure
Because more findings always look better in a report
Because the drill is required to produce at least one finding by policy
questions.explain: The same principle from the original incident applies here: a real number, even an imperfect one, found on a controlled schedule beats an untested assumption.
